item.description:

Ex-FBI employees charged with lying to Congress over Hunter Biden inquiries
October 23, 202611:51 AM ET
Ryan Lucas
Hunter Biden, son of former President Joe Biden, seen in July 2024 in Washington, DC.
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
hide caption

Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees with making false statements to Congress in connection with the bureau's investigations into Hunter Biden.
Bradley Benavides, 56, and Nikki Floris, 46, each face a single criminal count stemming from testimony before lawmakers in 2023. They were charged by complaint, which means prosecutors have yet to secure an indictment from a grand jury.
The laptop of Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden's son, was the subject of intense scrutiny after The New York Post reported weeks before the 2020 presidential election that the device was abandoned at a Delaware repair shop in 2019, and then obtained by President Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani.
Republicans have long accused the FBI of mishandling the laptop and the investigations into the younger Biden. Hunter Biden was convicted of federal gun charges and later pleaded guilty to separate tax offenses.

item.title: Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia
item.description:
Global Health
Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia
October 23, 202610:16 AM ET
By
Jonathan Lambert
One of the macaques at a Texas sanctuary, where researchers ran tests to see if the monkeys became germaphobes after experiencing a viral outbreak.
Stephan Kaufhold
hide caption
toggle caption i
Stephan Kaufhold
In the very early days of COVID-19, millions who'd rarely thought twice about germ avoidance became germophobes.
Some folks wiped down groceries before stuffing them into the refrigerator. Others let mail quarantine outside for days lest it harbor stray viruses. With the hindsight that SARS-CoV-2 spread primarily through the air, these sorts of precautions seem extreme. But in the moment, they were perhaps reasonable ways of avoiding an unknown pathogen.
Around this same time, a different virus hit a macaque sanctuary in Texas. New research suggests the monkeys responded in similar ways as humans did to COVID-19 — by being extra germophobic.
Humans are far from the only animals to avoid possible sources of disease. Scientists have found that critters as diverse as monkeys and nematodes (aka roundworms) can sense and steer clear of feces, for instance, which can harbor harmful bacteria.

Andri Tambunan for NPR
hide caption

Andri Tambunan for NPR
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
When Zyearre Amoah was a student at Sacramento State in 2023, there were times when he felt like the only Black student.
"There were African-American students on our campus," he recalls. But at a sprawling state university with more than 30,000 students, "it just felt like we had to look for each other."
Amoah graduated in 2024, just as his university was launching its Black Honors College, a school within a school with a special focus on Black history, life and culture. He's now a staff member at the BHC, as it's called, helping recruit students.
